text: The circuit and simulation layer from the previous lesson gives you two numbers for every outcome: an exact probability and an observed frequency. They're never going to match exactly — real shot-based sampling always has noise. This lesson builds the piece that decides, with actual statistics, whether a disagreement is ordinary noise or a genuine red flag.

Requirement four comes down to one statistical idea reused from Chapter 3: the standard error of a sampled proportion. For each outcome, validate computes the observed frequency, the expected statistical spread given the true probability and shot count, and flags it if the actual deviation exceeds n_sigma standard errors — three, by default.

Reuse the GHZ case: exact P(000) and P(111) at 0.5, 2048 shots, observed counts 1069 and 979. The standard error at p=0.5 and 2048 shots works out to 0.011049. The deviation for 000 is about 0.022, which divided by the standard error is roughly 1.99 — comfortably inside the 3-sigma range. This outcome should not be flagged, and the validator correctly leaves it alone — a deviation of about 2 standard errors is exactly the statistical wobble you expect from a finite sample.

Now contrast that with the Chapter 3 noisy Bell circuit: a 1% depolarizing error gave an observed frequency for 01 of about 0.0027 — small-looking in absolute terms. But the noiseless exact prediction says P(01) is exactly zero. There's no statistical universe where a perfectly noiseless circuit produces that outcome even once. This is exactly why the validator has a special case: when the exact probability is exactly 0 or 1, the standard-error formula breaks down, so any nonzero count on a theoretically impossible outcome gets flagged automatically, regardless of shot count.

Put the two cases side by side. The GHZ case had numbers that didn't match exactly but shouldn't be flagged, because the mismatch is well within ordinary randomness. The noisy Bell case had numbers that look small in absolute terms but absolutely should be flagged, because theory says that outcome is impossible and it happened anyway. A validator that only checked whether numbers looked close would get both of these backwards.

Next lesson writes the final piece of the spec — a gate-by-gate explanation of how the GHZ state actually evolved — and closes out the whole course by connecting every chapter back to this one small project.
